item.title: Floating nature islands installed in parks as Glasgow Games legacy
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a unique environmental project with useful vocabulary and context.

Floating nature islands installed in parks as Glasgow Games legacy

Floating islands are being installed on ponds in five of Glasgow's parks as part of the 2026 Commonwealth Games legacy.

The islands, which are being planted by community groups, are designed to encourage wildlife and help clean the water.

The project will create almost 250 square metres of new wildlife habitat which is expected to last about 20 years.

Glasgow 2026 organisers say they are funding the projects as part of their commitment to greener games.

The islands are manufactured by a Moray-based company which has been exporting them around the world.

Biomatrix Water Solutions in Forres has installed islands in Boston, Venice and London.

They have also been floated onto the River Clyde at the Glasgow Science Centre as part of an unrelated project.

The new islands are being installed at Victoria Park, Elder Park, Richmond Park, Queen's Park and Hogganfield Loch.

Ellen Hebdon, the company's operations manager, said the plants' roots played an important role in preventing and removing harmful algae from the water.

"It's not an overnight solution, but over a period of time, you will see benefits in the clarity and the cleanliness of the water," she said.

The islands are made up of recycled plastic materials, including drinking water pipes, to create buoyancy and are held together using marine-grade stainless steel.

They are then topped with a lightweight clay aggregate, called leca, into which the plants are inserted.

The aquatic plants include a mix of evergreen and flowering native species such as marsh marigolds, water forget-me-nots and ragged robin.

Their roots underneath the islands provide shelter for aquatic wildlife.

The location, in the middle of the water, also provides nesting spaces for birds, which would be largely free from disturbance.

Local schools and "friends of the park" groups are helping with the planting and maintenance.

Games organisers say sustainability is an important delivery factor with all competition venues powered by renewable electricity and electric or hybrid vehicles making up two thirds of the transport fleet.

Glasgow 2026's head of sustainability, Selina Donald, said the city council had been looking at creating floating islands but did not have the funding.

"I really saw the pride in all the parks, the pride in the green spaces, the pride in the natural environment across the city," she said. "And so really, for us, it was a way that we can celebrate and support that."

item.title: A fat-burning molecule has an unexpected benefit for your muscles
item.description:

Why it is here: Explains a scientific discovery with useful vocabulary and context for an English learner.

A fat-burning molecule has an unexpected benefit for your muscles

- Date:

November 26, 2026

- Source:

University of Leeds

- Summary:

Researchers have discovered that a naturally occurring molecule released during exercise helps muscles become stronger, resist fatigue, and withstand damage. The molecule, already available as a dietary supplement, could open new avenues for treating muscle deterioration associated with type 2 diabetes.

- Share:

Researchers have identified a naturally occurring molecule that plays a crucial role in building muscle strength and improving physical performance. Released during exercise, the molecule could also provide the basis for future treatments to protect against muscle damage associated with type 2 diabetes.

The molecule, known as L-β-aminoisobutyric acid (L-BAIBA), is essential for muscles to adapt to physical activity. It helps muscles become stronger, improves their resistance to fatigue, and protects against damage and weakness.

The study, published in Nature Communications and funded by Diabetes UK and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), reveals that L-BAIBA is a central regulator of the biological changes that allow muscles to improve their strength, structure, and endurance in response to exercise training.

How Exercise Triggers a Natural Muscle Booster

Although the health benefits of exercise are well established, scientists still do not fully understand the biological processes that allow the body to adapt to physical demands. A research team led by Professor Lee Roberts at the University of Leeds investigated whether these processes could reveal new ways to treat chronic conditions such as type 2 diabetes.

L-BAIBA has attracted scientific interest for more than a decade. In research published in 2014, Roberts demonstrated that the molecule has beneficial effects on metabolism, helping to enhance the body's ability to burn fat in response to exercise. L-BAIBA is now commercially available as a dietary supplement.

The latest findings reveal another important function of the molecule. L-BAIBA acts as a chemical messenger that connects physical activity with beneficial changes in muscle structure and metabolism, helping muscles adapt to the demands placed on them.

Lee Roberts, Professor of Molecular Physiology and Metabolism at the University of Leeds, said: "Our research identifies L-BAIBA as an exercise-induced signal that helps muscles adapt, improve their metabolic capacity and ability to contract, and ultimately enhances physical performance.

"This gives us exciting new insight into how exercise benefits the body and highlights a promising target for future therapies aimed at preserving muscle function in chronic conditions such as diabetes."

Protecting Muscles Against Damage From Type 2 Diabetes

The researchers also discovered that L-BAIBA protects muscles against damage associated with type 2 diabetes. The condition can negatively affect muscle health, leading to a decline in muscle mass and strength, as well as disruptions in the way muscles process and use energy. These complications can significantly reduce a person's quality of life.

Because regular physical activity is an important part of managing type 2 diabetes, finding ways to improve muscle function and reduce fatigue could make a substantial difference for people who struggle to exercise.

Type 2 diabetes is a serious chronic condition that increases the risk of potentially life-threatening complications, including heart attacks and strokes. Its development is influenced by a complex combination of factors, including age, ethnicity, genetics, and living with overweight or obesity.

Although type 2 diabetes has traditionally been more common among older adults, diagnoses in people younger than 40 have been rising in recent years. Cases in this younger age group are now increasing more rapidly than among adults over 40.

A Promising Target for Future Diabetes Treatments

Anna Morris, Assistant Director of Research Strategy and Partnership at Diabetes UK, said: "Exercise plays an important role in managing type 2 diabetes, but for many people muscle weakness and fatigue can make staying active a real challenge. This research helps us better understand how muscles adapt to exercise and identifies a potential new target for improving muscle health. While these findings are still at an early stage, they could help shape future approaches that support people with type 2 diabetes to remain active and live healthier, longer lives."

Although the discovery opens promising avenues for future treatments, further research is needed to determine whether L-BAIBA supplementation can produce meaningful therapeutic benefits in people with type 2 diabetes.

The research was led by the University of Leeds in collaboration with:

- Harvard Medical School, United States

- University of São Paulo, Brazil

- Wageningen University, Netherlands

- Newcastle University, United Kingdom

The study was funded by Diabetes UK and BBSRC.

item.title: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Important research on screen time and children with useful vocabulary and context.

Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time

- Date:

November 26, 2026

- Source:

Zhejiang University

- Summary:

Scientists have identified two potentially critical periods when screen time may be especially detrimental to children's learning and memory: infancy and the start of formal schooling. Greater screen exposure during these developmental windows was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later.

- Share:

Screen time at certain ages may be more closely tied to children's future learning and memory than previously recognized. A new study tracking children from age 1 to 8 found that those who spent more time watching screens during infancy and around the start of elementary school tended to perform worse academically at age 9 and have weaker working memory at age 10.5.

The findings suggest that when children use screens may be just as important as how much time they spend in front of them. Two ages in particular, 1 and 6, emerged as potentially sensitive periods in childhood development.

As digital devices become an increasingly common part of childhood, understanding their potential long-term effects has become a growing priority. Recommendations from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the American Academy of Pediatrics generally emphasize avoiding screen exposure during the first 18 to 24 months of life and limiting it to less than one hour a day for children ages 2 to 5. However, many young children spend considerably more time using screens.

Tracking Screen Time Throughout Childhood

Despite growing concerns about children's digital habits, previous research has produced mixed findings about the relationship between screen time and cognitive development. Many earlier studies examined children at a single point in time, concentrated on children already attending school, or did not regularly track screen habits throughout early childhood.

Following the same children over several years allows researchers to investigate whether screen exposure at particular ages is more strongly associated with later outcomes. This approach can also help researchers better account for the influence of family circumstances and environmental factors.

Scientists from Inserm and the National University of Singapore addressed these gaps in a study published in the World Journal of Pediatrics. The researchers examined data from 502 children participating in the Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcomes (GUSTO) birth cohort.

Parents reported their children's screen viewing habits at six different points between infancy and middle childhood. The researchers then evaluated the children's academic achievement and working memory several years later.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and manipulate information. It plays an essential role in everyday learning, allowing children to follow instructions, solve math problems, understand sentences, and keep track of information while completing tasks.

Two Ages Stand Out for Screen Time Risks

The researchers found that greater screen exposure at certain stages of childhood was associated with lower academic achievement and poorer working memory later in life. These relationships were particularly consistent among children who spent more time watching screens at age 1 and around age 6, when formal schooling typically begins.

Children who accumulated more screen time throughout childhood also tended to achieve lower academic scores. However, the strength of the associations varied depending on when the exposure occurred, suggesting that some developmental stages may be more sensitive than others.

One possible explanation is that screen viewing can take time away from activities that support cognitive development, including conversations with caregivers, imaginative play, and hands-on exploration of the physical world. These experiences provide opportunities for children to develop language, attention, memory, and problem-solving skills.

"The effect sizes we saw at age 1 were the largest among all time points we examined," the authors said. "That suggests early infancy may be a window of heightened sensitivity, when the developing brain is particularly vulnerable to the displacement of learning interactions by screen time. We were also surprised to see that while screen use at age 2 and 3 did not show significant links, the associations re-emerged at age 6 -- when children enter formal schooling. So it is not just about early years; screen use later in childhood still matters."

Although the study identifies associations rather than proving that screen time directly causes poorer cognitive or academic outcomes, the results highlight the potential importance of managing children's screen habits at different ages.

Why Even Small Differences in Screen Time Matter

According to the researchers, the results reinforce the principle that "less is better" when it comes to children's screen time.

An additional hour of daily screen viewing may not produce a noticeable difference in an individual child's academic abilities. However, when similar patterns occur across a large population, even relatively small differences in average performance could increase the number of children who experience academic difficulties.

The researchers suggest that efforts to encourage healthier screen habits could begin during infancy, with renewed emphasis around the transition to elementary school. This approach recognizes that children's developmental needs continue to change well beyond their toddler years.

The authors also stress that the amount of time children spend in front of screens is only one part of a much larger picture. Future studies should investigate whether the quality of digital content, the types of devices children use, and whether parents watch and interact with their children during screen time influence developmental outcomes.…

item.title: Harvard’s tiny UV light chip could help shrink quantum computers
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Technical but accessible article on a quantum computing breakthrough with useful vocabulary.

Harvardâs tiny UV light chip could help shrink quantum computers

- Date:

November 26, 2026

- Source:

Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences

- Summary:

Harvard-led researchers have developed a microscopic device that generates 120 times more ultraviolet light than previous comparable approaches by efficiently converting red light into UV. The breakthrough could unlock smaller quantum computers, ultra-precise atomic clocks, and compact environmental sensors.

- Share:

Ultraviolet (UV) light is already essential to a wide range of modern technologies. Beyond its natural presence in sunlight, it is used to disinfect surfaces, make biological materials fluoresce, and manufacture computer chips through a process called photolithography. In the future, microscopic sources of UV light built directly into photonic chips could enable smaller quantum computers, ultra-precise atomic clocks, and other advanced technologies.

However, shrinking UV light sources to fit on a chip has presented a significant engineering challenge. Ultraviolet light rapidly loses power as it travels through optical waveguides, the tiny channels that carry light across a chip. This limitation has made it extremely difficult to develop compact UV sources with enough power for practical applications.

Now, a Harvard-led research team has demonstrated a microscopic photonic device that produces approximately 120 times more UV power than previous comparable devices. The researchers, working in the laboratory of Marko Lončar, the Tiantsai Lin Professor of Electrical Engineering, achieved the breakthrough using a widely studied material called thin-film lithium niobate.

Published in Nature Communications, the findings establish lithium niobate as a promising platform for generating powerful ultraviolet light in compact devices while minimizing optical losses.

Turning Red Light Into Ultraviolet Light

Rather than trying to deliver ultraviolet light directly through microscopic channels, the researchers designed a device that generates UV light from red light within the chip itself.

The approach relies on a process known as frequency upconversion. Inside the lithium niobate crystal, two photons of red light combine to produce a single ultraviolet photon with higher energy. Lithium niobate is particularly well suited to this process because of its exceptional ability to convert light from one frequency to another.

"Our group is perhaps best known for utilizing lithium niobate for photonic devices that operate at longer, infrared wavelengths -- closer to the realm of telecommunications signals," Lončar said.

However, the team found that this transparent crystalline material, which has become increasingly important in integrated photonics, can also support light sources and guide light at much shorter wavelengths, including those in the ultraviolet range.

"When people think about [thin-film lithium niobate], they don't think of it as a UV material, but we show that it is," said co-first author Kees Franken, former research fellow in the Lončar lab. "We also show that there are some other nonlinear effects happening that we don't fully understand yet."

A New Technique Overcomes a Major Engineering Barrier

The device uses optical waveguides, microscopic channels etched into the lithium niobate film that direct light through the chip in much the same way electrical wires carry current.

For red light to be efficiently converted into ultraviolet light, the orientation of regions within the crystal must be repeatedly reversed at precisely controlled intervals along the waveguide. This manufacturing process, called poling, is a specialized technique used in nonlinear optics.

One of the biggest challenges has been creating these patterns with accuracy at scales smaller than a micrometer across devices that extend for centimeters.

Previous manufacturing methods required researchers to make an undesirable compromise. Poling the entire film before forming the waveguides made it difficult to correct manufacturing imperfections. Alternatively, creating the waveguides first reduced conversion efficiency because the electrodes were positioned too far away, allowing only part of the film to be successfully poled.

To eliminate this tradeoff, the Harvard team developed a technique they call "sidewall poling."

Precision Engineering Dramatically Improves Light Conversion

Instead of positioning the electrodes exclusively above the lithium niobate film, the researchers placed precisely patterned metal structures resembling tiny fingers directly alongside the etched waveguide. During fabrication, they applied a small voltage to permanently reverse the orientation of the crystal domains in a carefully controlled pattern.

"The key idea was: could we just put the electrodes directly on the waveguide?" said co-first author and former graduate student Soumya Ghosh. "It's a high-precision fabrication process to position the electrodes but requiring about 50-nanometer accuracy."

This arrangement enabled the researchers to reverse the crystal domains throughout the entire cross section of the waveguide, allowing light traveling through the material to undergo much more efficient frequency conversion.

The team could also fine-tune the spacing of the reversed crystal regions along the device. By incorporating existing "adapted poling" techniques previously developed in Lončar's laboratory and elsewhere, the researchers compensated for variations in the thickness of the lithium niobate film and the shape of the waveguide.

A 120-Fold Increase in Ultraviolet Power

The resulting device generated 4.2 milliwatts of ultraviolet power directly on the chip at a wavelength of 390 nanometers. That represents approximately 120 times the output power achieved by the best previous thin-film lithium niobate devices operating in this wavelength range.…

item.title: Why molecular cage catalysts show enormous differences in performance
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical article on molecular cage catalysts with useful vocabulary.

Why molecular cage catalysts show enormous differences in performance

Chemistry researchers have developed a new way to identify and understand highly effective artificial enzyme-like catalysts using powerful "molecular cages" that mimic the behavior of nature's enzymes. These tiny, hollow molecular structures act like miniature reaction chambers to trap molecules and accelerate chemical reactions. The cages showed enormous differences in performance, with the best catalysts more than 10,000 times more active than the least effective ones.

Researchers from the universities of Birmingham, Edinburgh and Oxford outline how they combined machine learning with a rapid screening technique in their article published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society.

Rather than preparing and testing each candidate catalyst individually, the research team, led by Professor Paul Lusby from the University of Edinburgh, developed a rapid screening approach allowing cages to be assembled and assessed immediately in solution. This allowed them to evaluate 30 distinct palladium-based molecular cage structures in a single study.

Co-author Dr. Jamie Lewis, an expert in cages and Royal Society university research fellow at the University of Birmingham, said, "Traditionally, discovering better cage catalysts has relied heavily on laborious trial-and-error experimentation and computationally expensive modeling. In this work we show how we can speed up this process to rapidly identify new catalytic cages."

Catalysts are essential to modern manufacturing, enabling about 90% of all chemical manufacturing processes worldwide. They are used to produce medicines, fuels, fertilizers, plastics and countless everyday products.

Dr. Laura Bickerton, a postdoctoral researcher in Lusby's group, who led the experimental component of the study, said, "This method allows us to access and investigate a wide range of molecular cages that would otherwise be difficult to isolate and study, giving us new insights into how we can tune catalyst functionality."

The experimentally measured cage reaction rate data were subsequently analyzed with AI and machine learning by professor Fernanda Duarte's group at the University of Oxford to understand why some cages worked as catalysts much better than others.

"We describe cages using physically motivated features that capture their shape, size, volume and electrostatics. Machine learning can correlate such features with reactivity, leading to a model with remarkable accuracy," said co-author Dr. Tomasz Piskorz, a postdoctoral researcher in the Duarte group who led the computational efforts.

The AI model identified key design principles that help the cage to be most effective as a catalyst:

- Compact, rigid cages performed best as catalysts.

- The precise arrangement of metal atoms inside the cage was more important than the overall size of the cavity.

- The electrical environment inside the cage helped to make it easier for the reaction to occur.

- Machine-learning models were able to accurately predict catalytic performance from structural features of the cages.

- Subtle differences in the angles between parts of the cage structure were among the strongest predictors of catalytic activity.

More efficient catalysts can reduce energy consumption, improve yields and decrease waste production, supporting net-zero and sustainability goals across industries including pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals and advanced materials. The research provides a route to designing such catalysts more efficiently.

Publication details

Laura E. Bickerton et al., Expanding Chemical Space Enables Data–Driven Structure–Activity Relationships in Cage Catalysis, Journal of the American Chemical Society (2026). DOI: 10.1021/jacs.6c11940

Journal information: Journal of the American Chemical Society

item.title: DESTINY model tracks molecular chemistry on uneven, ice-covered grains in interstellar space
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical article on astrochemistry with useful vocabulary.

DESTINY model tracks molecular chemistry on uneven, ice-covered grains in interstellar space

Interstellar space is the scene of active chemical processes: molecules form there in the gas, but also on the surface of tiny dust grains covered in ice. To better represent what happens on these surfaces, astrophysicists at the University of Liège are proposing a deterministic approach based on Markov chains with absorbing states, a mathematical tool that had not yet been utilized in astrochemistry. The paper is published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

Research in astrochemistry is organized into several branches. Astronomers measure molecular abundances using telescopes, laboratories replicate the conditions of the interstellar medium to study physical and chemical processes, and theoretical chemists focus on specific molecules or reactions. Kinetic models (models that calculate how the quantities of different molecules change over time, based on the rate at which the processes that create or destroy them occur) bridge the gap between these approaches. They use parameters derived from experiments and calculations to predict abundances, which are then compared with observations.

Infrared spectra recently obtained by the James Webb Space Telescope confirm that the chemistry on the surface of the grains and the resulting population of species are extremely complex, making it necessary to incorporate this chemistry more realistically into the models.

"On a grain, the chemistry results from a delicate balance between adsorption—when molecules from the gas settle on the surface—and a series of surface processes such as diffusion or encounters between reaction partners, as well as desorption, when molecules leave the grain to return to the gaseous phase," explain Maria Groyne and Cedric Baijot, FNRS Ph.D. students supervised by Michaël De Becker, an astrophysicist and director of the MEGA Laboratory at ULiège. "The deterministic models published to date already describe these mechanisms, but at the cost of two significant approximations."

The first concerns the surface itself. In the extremely cold conditions of the interstellar medium, the ice covering the grains is not crystalline but amorphous. Its surface is disordered and offers binding sites of varying strength depending on the local environment. Most models, however, assign only a single binding energy to each chemical species. The second approximation relates to interactions between molecules: in the standard formalism, two species present on the surface only influence each other when they react. Yet a simple encounter can alter the strength with which a molecule is bound to the surface.

"The DESTINY model, which we have developed entirely from scratch, overcomes these two simplifications," explains Baijot, an FNRS Ph.D. student at ULiège. "The model classifies surface sites according to their binding energy and, in a deterministic manner, tracks the possible path of each adsorbed species. At each stage, the species may remain in place, diffuse to another site, react with a partner or leave the surface. Markov chains with absorbing states enable these competing outcomes to be handled in a consistent manner."

Like on a dance floor

The researchers use the image of a dance floor to illustrate their approach. In classical models, all the tiles on the floor are identical, and the molecules—which play the role of dancers—behave in the same way everywhere. Two dancers who meet and dance together represent a chemical reaction.

"With DESTINY, the dance floor becomes uneven," explains Groyne, an FNRS Ph.D. student. "Some tiles are sticky, others slippery, and two identical dancers may meet different fates depending on where they are. The mere presence of another dancer can also alter the possible movements, without any reaction taking place. This is the case with dihydrogen: an encounter between two H₂ molecules can set one of them in motion, or even eject it into the gaseous phase."

Initial analyses show that the population of a single species is distributed across sites with varying energy levels, which influences surface chemistry. The team considers the trends observed for methane to be encouraging compared with previous models. These results will need to be investigated further. "This opens a new door to deterministic astrochemical modeling in the solid phase," emphasizes De Becker, "with prospects that we are only just beginning to explore."

This work is primarily fundamental research. It aims to improve our understanding of the chemistry of the interstellar medium and, in the longer term, to shed light on questions such as the origin of molecules associated with life or the complexity of molecules that may form elsewhere in the universe. "Because it describes chemistry on solid and irregular surfaces, the model could also, in the long term, be applied to other environments, such as natural aerosols present in Earth's atmosphere or that of Mars," conclude the study's authors. This avenue remains to be explored.

A Markov chain describes something that transitions randomly from one state to another, following a simple rule: the probability of the next step depends only on the current state, not on the path taken to reach it. The Game of the Goose is a good example. At each turn, the square you land on depends on the roll of the dice and the square you are currently on. Squares visited previously do not matter. Each square is a "state," and the dice determine the probabilities of moving from one state to another. This is known as "memorylessness": the present is sufficient to predict the future.

An absorbing state is one from which you can never escape. In the Game of the Goose, this is the finishing square: once reached, the game is over. These chains allow us to calculate the probability of ending up in each of the final outcomes, and how many steps it takes on average to get there.

item.title: Chromosome ‘glue’ could boost fertility by stabilizing ageing eggs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical article on fertility treatment with useful vocabulary.

Researchers have engineered a ‘molecular glue’ that can stabilize chromosomes in ageing mouse eggs1. They say their artificial cohesion system could pave the way for improved fertility treatments for women over the age of 35.

Chromosomes in animal eggs are held together by protein structures called cohesins. These help to ensure that chromosomes divide correctly during the process of cell division. But the level of cohesins declines as women age, which can cause chromosomes to separate early and be distributed incorrectly. The resulting eggs can have too many or too few chromosomes, a condition known as aneuploidy, which is a cause of infertility, failed in-vitro-fertilization (IVF) treatments and early pregnancy loss, particularly in women who are more than 35 years old.

To prevent this premature separation of chromosomes in eggs, Melina Schuh, a biochemist at Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences in Göttingen, Germany, and her colleagues designed an artificial system called TALhesin. The system uses engineered proteins that attach to regions of the chromosome in which cohesin is usually present, these proteins then bind to one another.

Many groups are trying to understand cohesin because it diminishes as women age, affecting fertility, says Bettina Mihalas, a reproductive biologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, but this is the first approach to replace the protein’s function with an engineered system. “It’s a very creative, well-engineered and well-thought-out approach,” she says.

The findings were published in Science on 26 November.

Genetic instructions

The researchers injected messenger RNA that encoded the engineered proteins into immature mouse eggs. The mouse eggs then produced the proteins. Using fluorescence microscopy imaging, the researchers confirmed that the TALhesin proteins attached to chromosome regions in which natural cohesin is normally lost.

The artificial system reduced the frequency of early chromosome separation in older mice aged 13 months, 17 months and 20 months compared with untreated eggs. In 17-month-old mice, the proportion of eggs without any premature chromosome-separation errors increased from 46.7% to 74.1% in those treated with TALhesin, similar to what is observed in eggs from young mice.

Chromatids — the two identical halves formed by a replicating chromosome — must separate at the right time during cell division. To enable this, the researchers added a ‘molecular scissor’ into their artificial system. This switched off the artificial cohesion system at the appropriate time.

Human chromosomes

The team have adapted the system to deliver engineered proteins that attach to regions of human chromosomes in which cohesin is usually present.

Experiments in donated human eggs showed that the TALhesin proteins accumulated in these regions. The researchers also found that chromosomes with high levels of the engineered proteins tended to have smaller distances between chromatids. This demonstrates that the TALhesin system holds the chromosomes together.

item.title: Orangutans face bleak future after Indonesia’s devastating wildfires
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important environmental issue with useful vocabulary and context.

For most of October, parts of Indonesia felt dystopian as wildfires turned the sky a reddish orange.

“It felt like you were on Mars,” says Erin Vogel, a primatologist at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey.

Vogel was visiting the Tuanan Orangutan Research Station in Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, at the time. She and her colleagues have been conducting research on the critically endangered Bornean orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus) there for more than 20 years, but this trip she spent much of her time fighting fires. There were roughly 300,000 blazes in the region between July and October, and October’s level of toxic particulate matter in the air was roughly 400 times higher than what the World Health Organization deems safe.

Indonesia is experiencing one of its most severe fire and haze season of the past three decades, in part because a super El Niño has dried out vegetation and brought winds that fuelled the flames. More than 2.8 million hectares have burnt across Indonesia so far, and Kalimantan has been affected the worst. Fires devoured 60% of Bornean orangutans’ habitats in Kalimantan, including healthy forests such as those at the Tuanan research station and in Gunung Palung National Park.

Nature spoke to Vogel about the disaster and what it means for orangutans. At the time of the interview, fires were still smouldering in Tuanan peat swamp forests.

What was it like at the Tuanan research station during the peak?

It was depressing and horrid. I’ve never seen so much forest loss in the 23 years I have worked in Indonesia. In the sky, there was this orange-brown haze that was very thick and it burnt your lungs if you weren’t wearing a respirator.

When I arrived in Tuanan, it really struck me how quiet the forests had become. You didn’t hear birds; you didn’t hear insects; you didn’t hear anything except trees burning and falling.

The forest staff, the orangutan staff, the phenology staff and the fire teams were all fighting fires. I felt in awe of those heroes voluntarily fighting these fires day and night. They’d all been doing so for more than two months straight. It takes real strength to be able to do that and not give up, and our team is just so positive and hopeful.

How have the fires affected the orangutans?

We saw some orangutans who seemed to be very lethargic and sick. We came across one of the males we’ve been studying for more than 15 years, and he was on the ground, breathing heavily. But when we saw him a couple of days later, he seemed to have recovered a little bit. He was near the research station, eating some vegetation on the ground, climbing trees and eating fruits. That reassures us that he is doing better.

We’re seeing orangutans being displaced from one area to others. That means we’re going to have competition between individuals over limited resources. That’s also going to change their behaviour. It’s going to be interesting to see what happens.
